claims.text: Conventional stainless steel relies on passive oxide layers for corrosion protection.
Passive oxide layers on stainless steel degrade under extreme chloride-containing or molten-salt conditions.
A machine-learning workflow integrating composition, processing, and corrosion data can predict optimal HEA-film deposition parameters.
A refractory HEA film can be deposited on a stainless-steel substrate.
HEA-film deposition on stainless steel can produce a nanocrystalline coating with a refined grain structure.
The nanocrystalline HEA film forms a dense and adherent barrier layer on stainless steel.
Machine-learning optimization of the HEA coating creates a self-healing, compact, and protective layer.
The optimized HEA coating limits elemental leaching.
The optimized HEA coating impedes the transport or action of corrosive species.
The HEA coating preserves stainless-steel surface integrity in high-temperature chloride-containing or molten-salt environments.
A machine-learning-optimized HEA film will significantly reduce the corrosion rate of stainless steel relative to unmodified stainless steel.
The corrosion improvement will be observable as lower weight loss.
The corrosion improvement will be observable through improved electrochemical performance.
The HEA coating will increase surface hardness relative to unmodified stainless steel.
Conventional trial-and-error coating processes produce less-refined or less-adherent coatings and higher corrosion rates than machine-learning-optimized deposition.
The coating's efficacy may vary between molten salts and high-temperature chloride solutions.
Factors omitted from the machine-learning model may reduce coating adhesion or stability at extremely high temperatures.
Existing HEA-coating studies demonstrate improved corrosion resistance on stainless-steel substrates.
